terms.comment: Both words are classical, and obscēnus has the sense “indecent, obscene” in Cicero (jocandī genus … obscēnum, Off. 1.104, Lewis & Short); we have found no classical instance of the phrase itself.

evidence: Quint. 8.3.38: sī obscēna nūdīs nōminibus ēnūntientur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To talk dirty is obscēna dīcere; Cicero: quodque facere turpe nōn est, modo occultē, id dīcere obscēnum est (Off. 1.127, Lewis & Short).
Morgan–Owens’s phrase; Lucilius uses it of words of ill omen, the adjective’s first sense.

phrases.latin: quodque facere turpe nōn est, modo occultē, id dīcere obscēnum est
phrases.english: and what is not shameful to do, provided it is done in private, is obscene to talk about

sources: Lewis & Short: obscenus · Lewis & Short: sermo · Lewis & Short: turpiloquium
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 304.
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. profanity.
